title: Gothika
full_review:
Late in Mathieu Kassovitz's stylish psychological thriller "Gothika" (Warner Bros.), its frayed heroine declares that "logic is overrated." Given the narrative incoherence of much of the movie, it is an opinion obviously shared by the filmmaker.

In "Gothika," Kassovitz navigates the murky nether regions of the human mind, crafting a gloomy tale of murder and sexual depravity with a supernatural twist. Yet, despite some white-knuckle moments, the plot meanders rather than moving chillingly toward its climax. And while Kassovitz proves adroit at creating suspense and keeping the audience's ice-cold sweat on a slow drip -- eschewing buckets of blood in favor of a more suggestive spookiness -- it quickly becomes apparent that the film's eerie neo-gothic moodiness is merely a diversionary tactic to distract viewers' attention from the poverty of the script.

Hale Berry plays Dr. Miranda Grey, a criminal psychologist working in the psychiatric ward of a dreary women's prison where her husband (Charles Dutton) is the chief administrator. Reason is the ruling principle of Miranda's life, a trait established in the film's opening scene where she dismisses the satanic rants of one of her patients (Penelope Cruz) as the ravings of a troubled mind, only to later discover the dark truths they conceal.

But after a mysterious encounter with an enigmatic girl while driving home through a rainstorm, Miranda wakes up on the other side of the glass -- literally -- finding herself an inmate in the asylum and the prime suspect in her husband's gruesome murder.

Left with only fractured memories of the night in question and haunted by ghostly visions of the roadside specter, Miranda begins to methodically piece together what really happened. Robert Downey Jr. plays a fellow jailhouse shrink who is attracted to his former colleague and who helps her try to salvage her sanity. However, uncovering the truth requires that Miranda abandon her long-held rationalistic assumptions and surrender to phantasmagorical forces bent on using her as a pawn in exacting revenge for a series of unspeakable crimes left unpunished. And let's not forget "Gothika's" shaggy-dog ending -- or, better yet, let's.

Berry plays desperation well, effectively conveying Miranda's spiraling disorientation as she struggles to keep her mind from plunging into madness. Nevertheless, the role remains two-dimensional, rarely demanding more than alternating looks of confused shock or caged fear. And though viewers seeking a few honest screams aren't expecting Lady Macbeth, it helps if the audience has a vested interest in the protagonist's dilemma.

On a more morally troubling note, while the film portrays Miranda as a strong, intelligent professional, it is laced with subtle sexual imagery which objectifies rather than empowers women. For all its slick paranormal visuals, much of "Gothika" plays like a babes-behind-bars B-movie, complete with a requisite group shower scene and sadistic-rapist subplot.

By far the film's most cinematically interesting element is the prison itself, with its crypt-like cellblocks and sepulchral corridors metaphorically mirroring the labyrinthine tangles of Miranda's twisted psyche. The shadow play of the incessantly flickering lights also contributes to the overall unsettling milieu. Unfortunately the creepy atmospherics can only carry the film so far. One can pardon hackneyed dark-and-stormy-night plot twists and wooden dialogue like, "I'm not delusional, I'm possessed," if the payoff is worth it; unfortunately, such is not the case here.

At one point Miranda's husband reminds her that sometimes people repress memories of bad experiences in order to spare themselves later psychological trauma; viewers of this film may do just that.

Due to some gory violence, flashes of shadowy nudity, as well as an instance of rough language and occasional crude language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
